newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-AMBITIOUS KOMEN SEEKS FIRST GOLD.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-AMBITIOUS KOMEN SEEKS FIRST GOLD.

text.p: After missing last year's Atlanta Olympics, Kenya's latest distance star Daniel Komen appears in his first major event confident he can take the 5,000 metres world title.

"Obviously, I was disappointed not to be in Atlanta," Komen, who failed to make his country's team for the Games, said on Monday. "I've never won a world title and that's my main goal this season. I'm looking forward to it."
His race last June in Nice, where he clocked the third fastest time ever in 12 minutes 48.98 seconds under pouring rain, made him the clear favourite for Sunday's final.

"It's something new for me," said Komen, who had a remarkable season last year, winning the overall Grand Prix title and taking more than four seconds from Algerian Noureddine Morceli's 3,000 metres world record by running in 7:20.67 last September in Rieti.
"It's not like in a meeting, here you have to go past three rounds and anything can happen," he added. "But I feel strong and I have an excellent team to help me."

Because of a controversial selection policy, Kenya's contingent in Athens does not look quite as impressive as in the past. But it is still good enough to provide Komen with all the support he will need.
To make sure he can rely on the help of compatriots Tom Nyariki and Paul Bitok, Komen must emerge as his team's strongest asset after the qualifying rounds.

"That's the way is goes," he explained. "In the final, the one who proved he deserved to be the leader can count on the others. The goal is to win gold for Kenya. There is a strategy but it's secret. An army that goes to war does not reveal its tactics."
At only 21, Komen is already walking in the footsteps of his idol Kip Keino, arguably the biggest name in Kenya's rich history of distance runner.
"When I was a kid, I used to dream I would be like Keino," said Komen, whose background his similar to the one of the man he admires most.
He grew up in Nyaru, outside Eldoret, the Rift Valley town made famous by Keino. From the age of eight, he ran 20 kilometres every day going to school and back home.
"I did not know I was doing training," he said.
According to his idol, Komen has a bright future ahead of him: "He has not reached his potential yet," Keino said.
Last year after the Grand Prix final in Milan, Komen was unprepared for the awards ceremony, having packed only a scruffy-looking costume he had picked up in Eldoret.
He was taken to a shop nearby where he was fitted for an expensive designer's suit. "He looked very nice," Keino remembered.

Now ready for success, Komen, whose chances of a gold medal improved even more when Ethiopian rival Haile Gebrselassie decided to concentrate on the 10,000 metres, has made sure he would be smart enough this time.
